### 8. Comforting Treatise on the Four Temperaments

<meta>The catchword "menti" likely refers to the Latin "temperamenti" or "complexioni," continuing the thought from the previous page.</meta>

...unkenness, you have a dangerous path here through the sea of misery in this temperament <note>Böhme is now describing the Phlegmatic temperament, which he associates with the element of Water and a tendency toward being easily influenced by external "reflections."</note>; you will always be stained by the vices of words and deeds.

117. Water has a bright luster within it and produces a reflection, yet it is a false mirror. Likewise, the poor soul has a nearly unjust mirror in this temperament: for water takes everything into itself, whether it be evil or good; it holds it, and becomes clouded by it.

118. So it goes also with this temperament: it absorbs the poisonous rays of all the stars and presents them to the poor, imprisoned soul as a mirror. The soul then takes the bait <note>original: "beisset sie dann" — literally "bites into it," like a fish catching a hook.</note> and carries out in the body that which is merely a magical mirror within the temperament.

119. O, what good, sweet words—like sweet water—are offered for free, yet are full of bitter gall mixed in by the stars. There is almost no amount of deceit that is too much: lies are the cloak of hypocrisy, used to display oneself with a mirrored luster. Where "good Christians" dwell in <term>Babel</term> <note>original: "Babel" — In Böhme's writing, Babel represents the "city of confusion" or the corrupt, institutionalized church that values outward appearance over spiritual truth.</note>, this is and wants to be counted as divine service.

120. You do not notice that you are doing wrong, but if someone comes too close to you with even a tiny spark, it is immediately reflected in your mirror. You would be well advised to recognize that you are an ever-sinful human being. You should enter into true repentance and pray to **God** for the guidance of His **Holy Spirit**, so that the evil impulses <note>original: "Affecten" — referring to emotional or astrological influences that move the will.</note> of the stars may be broken and kept in check, lest the poor soul embrace them and thus become a fool.

121. A sober life will also be healthy for you. Constant vigilance and prayer, and remaining always in the fear of God—this turns away all evil coming from the stars. For he who lives according to the stars lives just like the cattle. But if one fixes the fear of God into the heart, the soul becomes a master over the outward life and forces it into obedience. If this does not happen, however, the temperament becomes the master and guide of the soul. Although the temperament cannot rule the soul by its own power, it nevertheless presents the soul with its ele-

<summary>Böhme describes the Phlegmatic temperament as a "false mirror" of water that easily absorbs both good and evil influences from the stars. He warns the reader to overcome these external astral impulses through a sober life and constant "fear of God" to ensure the soul remains master over the body.</summary>

# IX. Way to Christ

...mental and stellar mirror, in which the soul gazes in wonder and allows itself to be captured. <note>Böhme concludes his warning about the Phlegmatic temperament, which he believes acts like a "mirror" reflecting the impulses of the stars (astrological or external influences) rather than divine truth.</note>

122. Therefore, a human should be a human, and not a beast; he should rule humanly with the soul, and not with the desire of the <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "Complexion" — in Böhme's philosophy, this refers to the physical and psychological makeup determined by the four humors. He argues that one must not be a slave to their natural personality type.</note>; thus he may attain the highest and eternal good, regardless of which temperament he is under.

123. There is no temperament so noble that—if a person only desires to live according to the stars—the devil would not find his pleasure within it. <note>Böhme warns that even "good" natural dispositions can be corrupted if they are directed toward worldly or astrological forces rather than the divine.</note>

124. Therefore, it is rightly said according to St. Peter's scripture: 1 Peter 5:8. "Be sober and watch, for your adversary, the devil, walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour": resist him in the fear of God, and never feel safe from him.
